source.title: An explainable transformer circuit for compositional generalization
source.authors: Cheng Tang; Brenden M. Lake; M. Jazayeri

record.tranche_reason: The paper cites induction-head work as background but studies a different behavior: compositional function induction in a synthetic task, not repeated-token induction or its formation during training.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own compositional-task performance and circuit interventions. These concern a related but different construct from the claim’s repeated-token induction behavior, so the rows are linked to none of the claim versions. The cited claims about induction heads are not treated as study results.
record.test_reason: The paper cites induction heads (Elhage 2021, Olsson 2022) only as background. Its results concern a task-specific circuit for compositional function induction in a 2+2-layer encoder-decoder transformer with MLPs. It reports no previous-token heads and no [A][B]…[A]→[B] copying. It does not track formation over training, loss against token index, or induction heads across models. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that a compact transformer solves compositional induction with an interpretable, causally validated QK circuit, and that activation edits guided by the circuit steer its behaviour predictably. They make no claim about canonical induction heads.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses causal circuit tracing, ablations, and activation swaps on a synthetic function-composition task, rather than testing the original repeated-token induction-head mechanism.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that multiple heads can compensate for one another: Dec-cross-1.1 and Dec-cross-1.3 partially compensate beyond the first three output tokens; it also reports distributed roles across similar-function heads.

fits_no_version.finding: A compact encoder-decoder transformer reaches 98% held-out accuracy on synthetic function composition. The authors trace this to a multi-head QK circuit carrying index-in-question and relative-index-on-LHS, confirmed by path patching, ablations and a position-embedding swap.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In-context compositional induction in small transformers can be implemented by a distributed multi-head circuit that aligns positional-index information, distinct from the canonical induction-head motif.

record.problems: The analysis is limited to one relatively small model and a synthetic task. The authors note that the activation swaps did not completely perturb predicted tokens because multiple heads have similar roles. Numerical R2 values and numerical outcomes for several ablations are not stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional task-specific circuit plots or attribution details are recorded beyond the primary performance, index-information, ablation, and activation-swap results above.

untested.parts: No previous-token head, no induction-head composition, and no repeated-token copying is measured. The model is an encoder-decoder with MLPs, not attention-only.
No training-time dynamics, phase change, or loss bump is reported. Only the final trained model is analysed.
There is no measure of in-context learning by token index and no large models.
Only one small model and one training run are studied, and induction heads are not identified.
Data and training setup are not varied.
The paper finds a task circuit for in-context composition, but never measures or ablates induction heads, so it gives no comparison with them.

record.verdict_notes: All row links to ['none'] are correct. r1 is a capability check rather than a claim result. The Question-Broadcast head attends from support symbols to their copies in the question, which resembles a duplicate-token head rather than an induction head, and the paper does not frame it as one.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test previous-token-head composition or the [A][B] … [A] → [B] copying mechanism.
Does not track induction-head formation, in-context-learning changes, or loss over training time.
Does not test whether induction heads explain most in-context learning in large transformers.
Does not test whether heads with the claim’s induction behavior occur across model families, sizes, training runs, architectures, or modalities.
Does not vary data or training setup to test their effects on canonical induction heads or in-context learning.
Does not distinguish few-shot task learning from repeated-token copying or compare their mechanisms.
Does not study developmental transitions in induction-head formation during training.
